utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, again, you do not appear to have listened to my question. What treatment did he require?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A cut on his head, because a police hit him on his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in the second paragraph of page 3 of your statement, and in the B/C/S and Albanian version it's paragraph 4, you say that you saw houses on fire. Where were those houses?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: These houses are in our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And my last question relates to the next paragraph in your statement -- no, sorry, that's not correct. It relates to the last paragraph on page 3 and paragraph 5 in -- excuse me. It does relate to the next paragraph in the statement. Sorry, Mr. Krasniqi, that's my mess, not you making any mistakes. Mr. Krasniqi, you say that you saw roadblocks, you passed roadblocks, as you were on your way to Albania. Who were manning those roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Those that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You mentioned both police and military earlier. Do you mean that there were both police and military at the roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. They were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That concludes my questions for the witness, Your Honour, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I am attorney-at-law Mihajlo Bakrac, one of the Defence team of General Lazarevic. The first thing that I would like to know, Mr. Krasniqi, is you mentioned giving two statements today; one on the 12th of March - later you corrected yourself, saying that it was in April 1999, and that correction we mentioned, in 2004; and finally the third statement -- in fact, additional information provided on the 12th of October. Did you give a statement on the 13th of December, 1999? Is there any other statement that you have given?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think this issue was dealt with in the filings that were made in the context of the 92 bis motion that was filed by the Prosecution. There exists another version of the statement which was signed by the witness in December 1999. The contents of the statement that is included in the 92 bis package and the contents of the statement that was signed in December are identical. There was a declaration filed by the investigator who took -- who participated in the signature of the statement in December 1999. It is found in the registry -- in the filings in the registry, page 6488, which explains the process by which it came about. But it's not a separate statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've given enough information for Mr. Bakrac now to proceed with the cross-examination, if he wants to deal with the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just wouldn't agree with my colleague, Mr. Marcussen, that they are identical. The statement included in the package bearing the date of the 12th is different to this other statement, and I will just state at the end of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By all means, explore the matter in cross-examination if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we are now talking about your statement of the 12th of March, 1999, that is, the date on the statement, or from April, as you say. Was that statement translated and read back to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it was read back to me in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the interpreter who read that back to you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know if that translated statement, since the interview was in English, was signed by the interpreter on the declaration?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Could you repeat it again, please. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the interpreter who did the interpreting for you, whose name you say you don't know, sign the translation of that statement, to the best of your knowledge, if you know? If you don't know, say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the statement included in the package there is no name of the interpreter. It just says "Interpreter." I checked both the English and the Albanian version and there is no signature of the interpreter. I don't know if the Prosecution can explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He won't be able to answer that for you, Mr. Bakrac, and it's a matter you can try and clarify with the Prosecution at some other stage. But I think for the moment you should concentrate on using your time to ask the questions you wish to ask of the witness. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe if I just may address one issue. My understanding is - and I agree with my colleague - the statement that was included in the 92 bis package was not a signed copy, but in September 2004, when the witness was met by a representative of the registry, he adopted the statement that is included in the 92 bis package. So I don't think there's -- I hope there isn't any issue about whether or not the statement that is included in the 92 bis package is, indeed, reflecting what the witness's evidence is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, according to Mr. Bakrac's -- in fact, according to your statement, Mr. Marcussen, you said that there exists another version of the statement which was signed by the witness in December 1999. Now, Mr. Bakrac's point relates to it not being signed by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm confirming that the statement that is included in the 92 bis package was not signed by -- is not the one that was signed by the witness in December. There are no signatures -- as I can see from the record, there were no signatures on the document that the witness signed in September 2004, prior to him signing or giving -- putting his initials on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by, "There exists another version of the statement which was signed by the witness in December 1999"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That there exists a statement that -- well, exactly that; that we have a statement which has ERN numbers K0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste time on this. Mr. Bakrac, if the statement you're dealing with is signed by the witness, you can deal with the question of interpreter's signature in discussion with the Prosecution later. But if you have questions to ask about a statement he signed in December 1999, you should use your time to do that and not deal with this administrative business.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that the Prosecution is baffled as well; I'm not the only one who's baffled. We got statements from the 12th of March and 13th of December, somewhat different from the statement included in the package which bears the date the 12th of March. In this official version of the statement we don't know who the interpreter was; there is no name and no signature of the interpreter. So we don't know whether this is a compilation of statements, maybe, or what it could be. The very beginning of these two statements are different. The statement bearing the dates of 12th March and 13th December were signed by the witness on the 13th of December, and they are not quite the same, contrary to what my colleague Mr. Marcussen says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you expect me to do about it, Mr. Bakrac, except let you ask questions about it, if you want to do it. There's nothing else I can do it. You're just using your time unnecessarily on debating this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will question the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement in Albania, in March?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, because on the 28th of March we left the country. It was not on the 12th; it was on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. Tell me, please, did you have occasion, on the 19th of September, 2004, to correct all the possible errors in your statement? Did the Office of the Prosecutor give you the opportunity, on the 19th of September, 2004, to correct anything that could have been incorrect in your statement?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I told them that the date is wrong, because the statement was not given on the 12th of March but on the 12th of April; and the place was Kruja and not Durres. I told them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you are saying to us now that, back in September 2004, you told the office of the Prosecutor, in fact you drew their attention to the fact, that it was not 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, right now I have in front of me your statement of the 19th of September, 2004, and I will read to you one sentence: "In the unofficial statement given to Jerry Saxon, investigator of the OTP, that has been read back to him today on the 19th of September, 2004, some errors were discovered that need to be corrected." And then you proceed to correct: Your personal details, the address has to be corrected; the interview location should be Kruja, not Drac; and where it says that the statement was read back to you in the Bosnian language, that should be corrected to read "Albanian language." So you told the Prosecution that the date of the first interview was not the 12th of March and they did not record it. Is that the way I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't on the 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, in 2004, on the 19th of September, you drew the attention of the Prosecution that it was not in March, on the 12th, it was in April. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that it was in April, not in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you think of any reason why the Prosecution did not record this, if you told them so, why they did not record it in the statement of the 19th of September, 2004?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a serious point to be pursuing, Mr. Bakrac? And is that a serious question for this trial, a trial of this magnitude? Please let's concentrate on things that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will move on, but I think that a serious trial of this magnitude should not allow such errors, all the more so because we don't know which statement holds true and where it was taken, whether in Albania or in other country. I think these are serious errors that should be corrected to uphold or to establish the authenticity of his statement. But I will move on. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you know that as of the 24th of March, 1999, Prizren was bombed? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 27th and the 28th the barracks of the Army of Yugoslavia in Prizren was bombed on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The first day, on the 24th, the army barracks in Prizren were bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there bombardments also on the 27th and 28th of March, not far from the building of the Municipal Assembly of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 28th of March you said you saw 50 or 60 tanks of the Army of Yugoslavia; were they camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you saw them. My question is: Were they camouflaged; and if so, if what way?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, they had things on top, a kind of net that they were covered in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So they were camouflaged, masked, covered. Are you aware that in those circumstances they are unable to move?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, when the tank is stationed somewhere and doesn't move, it's like that. But there were tanks that I saw moving, and came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you just saw some tanks coming there and stopping.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was it logical, in your view, that after the bombing of the barracks, tanks with anti-aircraft weapons on them have to be stationed somewhere?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, these things were talked about on the streets.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were deployed on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I -- no, I don't think -- I was going to ask you to perhaps assist us with the proper description of these vehicles, but I don't think that is appropriate, in the circumstances. That's a matter you'll, no doubt, deal with at a later stage. And can I take it that you're not, in fact, going to pursue anything in relation to the statement of the 13th of December, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to clarify that with my learned friends from the Prosecution, and depending on what I establish, I will give you a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if there's something in it that you think is contradictory of other evidence that the witness is giving, this is the only opportunity you have got to deal with that. So, can I take it there is nothing of that nature that you want to deal with in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you're right. There are no contradictions; there are just parts of one statement that are missing in the other. Otherwise, there are no discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Krasniqi. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I'm one of the Defence attorneys for Sreten Lukic. I have a number of questions for you here today, and I would ask you to pay close attention to each of my questions so as to try and give me the most truthful and concise answer possible, since we do need to try to finish up before the break. Now, sir, you are from the village of Dusanovo. Can you please tell us what the ethnic make-up of Dusanovo village was in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The village of Dushanova had all the nationalities there. There were Albanians, Serbs, and Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the approximate break-down percentage-wise of the population that was, for instance, ethnic Serb, ethnic Albanian, Roma, or Goran?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I never kept statistics. But what I know is that there were 40 Serb households or houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many Albanian households there were in that village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A lot of them. There are many Albanians. I don't know the exact number, but I know that there are many.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And could you please tell us a little bit about your employer Printex. How many ethnic Serbs and ethnic Albanians worked there in -- I should say, in February and March of 1999, if you know.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Are you asking me? Okay. Until 1999 -- Printex, I worked there for 34 years. So until 1999, it was about 50/50, Albanians and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in your statement, you state that there were tensions that occurred before the NATO bombing, and you set forth that your Serb colleagues said that if NATO started bombing, they would kill you. Now, when you talk about Serb colleagues, are you talking about your co-workers from the Printex factory?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. The military forces told us that. It was the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm looking at your statement --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- at the second page in all versions of your statement, so we can deal with the one that's in the 92 bis, and it clearly there states, when talking about the textile factory called Printex, where you worked in Prizren for 27 years, it says: "There were both Serbs and Albanians working there. I was never involved in politics. I am a Muslim. There was no tension in our neighbourhood before this. Then our Serb colleagues told us they would kill us if NATO started bombing them." And I'm trying to find out whether, in fact, your statement is accurate, that it was your Serb colleagues that told you that they would kill you if NATO started bombing, and then to find out what you mean by "colleagues." Are those the colleagues from Printex or are they your neighbours in the village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. On the 23rd - please understand me - our Serb colleagues, we left work together, and they told us that if NATO attacks, the soldiers had said they would kill us. Are you clear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to be clear, but it seems like you are changing it yet again. Did you actually witness anyone telling you that if NATO started bombing, they would kill you, or is this something that you heard from other people? I mean, did someone personally threaten you in this manner?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, let's not get into details. When we left work, we were going home -- because I understand Serbo-Croatian, and we were together with our Serb colleagues when the soldiers said, "If NATO attacks, then you will be killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it now your testimony that, in fact, your Serb colleagues were not the ones who made these statements but it was these soldiers who you've now identified for the first time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that is not set forth in the statement that you said was read back to you and that you agreed was the truth of what you knew and what you could testify to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Maybe I did not understand the statement well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that there are other portions of the statement that you did not understand well; that is to say, was the translation that was provided for you at the time that the statement was read back to you not very comprehensible to you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you some questions to try and clarify, then. Did you perceive hostility directed against the ethnic Albanian residents of your village by the ethnic Serb or other non-Albanian residents of the village, arising as a result of the foreseen NATO bombing campaign and the eventual commencement of that bombing?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you describe the situation in your village, in March of 1999, as being tense as a result of the impending NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, then, that after NATO started bombing, that all of a sudden the situation was tense in your village of Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after NATO started bombing, would you describe your village as also being tense due to KLA activities, if not within the village, in the surrounding area of the totality of the Prizren municipality?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of any KLA activity in the surrounding area of your village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Had you ever seen KLA present in the area surrounding your village or in your village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then, perhaps you could clear something up for me, because in your statement, although stating that there was no KLA activity in your area, you go on to describe the individuals that came wearing uniforms on the 28th of March, and in particular you describe persons wearing black combat uniforms with some kind of insignia on their arms, and then you also describe persons wearing blue camouflage uniforms "similar to the KLA." Now, if there was no KLA activity in your area, how could you have an appraisal of what kind of uniforms the KLA wore?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there, in fact, KLA in your area that dressed in blue camouflage uniforms, as is recorded in your statement, the type of blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, not the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about some activities that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're moving to something else, let me ask the witness something. Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, could you give the witness a hard copy of the Albanian and just mark the paragraph in which this reference occurs --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph of page 2 on the English, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know which paragraph it is. I just want Mr. Marcussen to mark where it is so that the witness can quickly read to us what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'll just see if I can identify the line so we get it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's just a paragraph. It starts with: "My brother and I had 60 ..." Now, Mr. Krasniqi, on that copy of your statement in Albanian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you'll see the paragraph that's marked now for your attention. Can you read the paragraph that's marked, please. Just read it aloud to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which part, once again? This one here, or here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did you mark it, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I underlined a sentence in red. I think that's the sentence Mr. President would like you to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one in red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They were wearing black combat uniforms with some kind of insignia. They were also wearing blue camouflage uniforms similar to the KLA. There was no KLA. Some of them were wearing masks --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there. You've read a part that says: "They were also wearing blue camouflage uniforms similar to the KLA." Did you say that to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I might have told the investigator that, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what information did you have about the KLA -- the uniforms that the KLA wore at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I didn't pay attention. I minded my own business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krasniqi, most people do generally mind their own business, but sometimes they also get information about the activities of importance that are happening in their area. Now, tell us, please, what information you had at that stage about the uniforms that were worn by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't describe it because I haven't seen them. I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why did you give that description to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After we finished, after it finished, I know that I've seen the KLA uniforms on TV and I thought they were similar with those uniforms that I had seen on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say that after it finished you saw the KLA uniforms on TV; however, in this statement you testified to, you gave it actually in April of 1999, which would have been just one -- less than a month after -- in fact, I think it's about two and a half weeks after you left your village. Did you see the KLA on TV at that time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, after I left my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to ask you a little bit more about your knowledge of things. First of all, are you -- Mr. Krasniqi, are you familiar with a man named Xhemshet Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Now it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- let me repeat that. Mr. Krasniqi, are you familiar with a man named Xhemshet Krasniqi, whose nom de guerre was Beli Medved, or White Bear, who was the KLA/UCK commander for the unit that covered the area between Vrbica to Zur to Ljubicevo to Jeskovo, up to Lez, to the very south-west border of Prizren city?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you not happen to see on TV or hear about the efforts undertaken by Mr. Xhemshet Krasniqi and Mr. Xhevat Berisha to blow up the St. George church in Prizren itself, even back in October 1997?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this, and I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you briefly about two other individuals who were KLA commanders in the area of the Prizren municipality where your village is located. Have you ever heard of --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: If you can speak a little bit louder because I can't hear well with one ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it's me or the translators that should speak louder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I think it must be the adjustment of the earphones that's required.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, sir?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Now it's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, I wanted to just briefly go through two other individuals who were KLA commanders in the Prizren municipality where your village is located to find out if you had heard or knew anything about them and their activities. A gentleman by the name of Rifat Sulejmani and a gentleman by the name of Ekrem Rexha, did you have occasion to hear about them or any of the activities of their units in the area where you lived in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Please, let the counsel be told that I never heard of these things and I have no knowledge whatsoever about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of certain weapons that were turned in by villagers from your village to the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to ask you a couple of questions, if you know, with respect to the population in your village. Is it correct that a portion of the population actually remained in the village and did not leave in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Those that remained went to the town. Nobody remained in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge -- upon returning to your village, did you have knowledge of any attacks undertaken by the KLA against villagers from your village who had remained in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to a teacher from Dusanovo, the father of a villager named Snjezana Djordjevic, who was attached to a tractor and pulled to his death, from Dusanovo village to the nearby vineyards, by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know anyone named Djordjevic in the Dusanovo village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is a large village, and I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And upon your return to Kosovo, did you have occasion to learn about the KLA killing of another villager from Dusanovo village, Djumret Pajaziti, himself a Goran, an ethnic Muslim?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have not heard about this. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you briefly discussed the bombings that occurred in Prizren after NATO air-strikes began. Am I correct that for four straight days, that is the 25th of March, 26th of March, 27th of March, and 28th of March, Prizren city itself was struck multiple times by NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The gun-fire was heard, the explosions were heard, but we don't know -- I don't know where the bombs actually fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On those evenings was there a -- was there electricity available after these explosions were heard?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you remember, sir, on the 28th of March, do you recall what time of day these forces that you've described arrived at your house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They came on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I asked you, sir, if you recall what time of day, on the 28th, these forces were --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They came at around 4.30, 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at that point in time, sir, were you able to clearly see the uniforms of the individuals that you have described as being police who were a part of this force that came to your house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you able to eye-witness any words that were uttered by these persons? For instance, when -- in your statement, on page 2, in the fourth paragraph, when you say, "Go to Albania. There is no place for you here in Kosovo," did you personally eye-witness who uttered those words?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not know that person who uttered those words, but younger people know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you close enough to that individual to see the specific details of his uniform, if, in fact, he was wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I could see the uniform because I met him, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, could you please describe that uniform for us in as much detail as you can.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how else to describe it. It is the same description that I gave earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've described black combat uniforms and then you've also described uniforms similar to those worn by the KLA. Which uniforms -- or was there a different type of uniform, sir? Which uniform is it that you described earlier that this person was wearing?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That was the police and a person with black clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did these black clothes have any insignia or labels; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were wearing black clothes, they had masks, and you could only see their fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did these black clothes have any markings on them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also discuss in your statement that at the time that these persons came to your home, you describe that they had police cars which had Prizren number plates. Now, these vehicles that you describe as police cars with Prizren number plates, are they separate from the vehicles you described earlier today that were armoured vehicles, or are we talking about the armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They are similar to those described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say they had Prizren number plates, am I to understand that to mean that the licence plates started with the letters PZ and then had a number following it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: PZ. I can't hear anything now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, these vehicles with the PZ licence plates, were they plain coloured, or did they have any other markings or emblems on them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The police vehicles that I saw with registration plate PZ, these were jeeps. And as for the other vehicles, I don't know where they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe you had earlier testified that you only saw tanks, armoured personnel carriers, and anti-aircraft pieces. Are you now telling us that there were also jeeps present on the road in your village on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They passed by the main road. They were passing by there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned certain injuries that were encountered by members of your family. Do you have any hospital documentation or was any hospital documentation issued for this treatment?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. We did not know that we will need them later. We didn't know at that time that there will be people who will want to shed light on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that the hospital in Albania did not provide medical documentation for you at any point in time --

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. We didn't even ask for that documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you also specify -- strike that. Am I correct that, with regards to your description of what transpired on the 28th of March, the evening hours of the 28th of March when these forces arrived to your home, is your knowledge of those events limited to what you saw at your own residence; that is to say, that you did not see what had happened elsewhere in the village which, you had testified to, was a rather large village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that ethnic Serbs had left that village as well, either that day or the night before? And you don't know why they left that village, do you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Krasniqi. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've completed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, just a few questions to clarify some matters that have come up. Mr. Bakrac, the first counsel who asked you questions, spoke to you about whether the tanks you saw at different points in time had camouflage on them, and you explained how they had been covered with -- on top of them, there was some sort of camouflage on the tanks. My question is: The tanks you saw in the street, did they also have camouflage on them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They had the same colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But did they -- on top of them, was there some sort of camouflage put on top of them?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They had some kind of leaves so that they would not be detected, I suppose, by the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And those leaves, were they attached to the tank itself?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Those tanks were not moving; they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But the leaves, were they attached to the tank?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no. They were kind of like an umbrella cover for the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were asked about your colleagues who told you that soldiers had said that you would be killed if the NATO started to bomb. What day was that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you feel scared by that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic asked you if the situation in your village became tense after the NATO bombing had started. Would you say that it was also fairly tense after your colleagues had told you that you would be killed if the NATO started to bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I asked and answered -- my question originally to him was relating to the period prior to the NATO bombing, and I believe he said it was not tense and it only became tense after the bombing, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the matter has been dealt with, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You described the different people who came to your house on the 28th of March, and there was some people in black uniforms and one of those told you that you should go to Albania. From what you could observe about how these different people were operating, was it your impression that they were working together?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: These persons acted in the same way. They wanted to massacre us, to expel us, and to send us to Albania as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did both people in blue uniform and people in black uniform enter your house?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Also people in green uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were soldiers as well, regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me hear the first objection. Mr. Aleksic, I think, was first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think this was referenced to in the statement or during the examination-in-chief or during the cross-examination, that some people went through his gate wearing green uniforms. This doesn't stem from either the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just to second that, Your Honour. And I wanted to say that this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On page 2, the third paragraph of the statement says, about the middle: "There were tanks with big 105-millimetre cannons on them. The police cars came from Prizren. There were tanks right outside my front gate. The army was also there, the VJ." My understanding of the statement is, indeed, that -- that they were all -- I'm sorry, it goes on at the end by saying: "All the street was sealed off by the police and the military." My understanding is that, indeed, the evidence has been that there were both police and military involved in this operation, and also that they came to the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing in the cross-examination from which the question you just asked could possibly derive; and secondly, it was a grossly leading question to which the answer would be of no value. For both these reasons, we sustain the objection and we'll ignore any comment made by the witness in response to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, that completes your evidence, brings it to an end. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give this evidence. That means that you are now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Rahim Latifi. He is also a 92 ter witness; he was previously a 92 bis (B) witness. His evidence is relevant to paragraph 72(b) of the indictment, as the last witness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Latifi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which is now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Latifi, we have before us statements that you've given and also a written copy of the evidence you gave when you were here before and were a witness in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, so we have a great deal of information about the case that you can give to us. The purpose of today's hearing is to enable counsel involved in the case to ask questions that they feel will assist us further. The first person to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecutor, and that will be Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please state your name to the Court so we shall have that right on record.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Rahim Latifi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Latifi, on the 28th of April, 1999, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after the statement had been taken, it was read back to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you were asked to sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you did sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And on the 29th of January, 2002, did you speak to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and the registry about your statement again?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you signed a declaration saying that your statement was correct. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And last week in Prizren, did you have an opportunity to read your statement again?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, I read it again last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is the statement a correct reflection of the events that you described in that statement?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's a true reflection of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So if you were asked to describe all those events again today, you would describe them as they are described in the statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, if you -- yes. If you were asked about the events that you described in your statement today, you would describe them as you have described them in your statement.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At this stage, Your Honour, I would like to tender the statement of Mr. Latifi as Exhibit P2381.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Latifi, did you also testify in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April, 2002, the transcript of that testimony, has that been read back to you recently?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, it was read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is it the case with that transcript, that if you were asked the questions you were asked in the Milosevic case, you would answer them in the same way as they are answered in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender, then, the exhibit -- sorry, the transcript from the Milosevic case as Exhibit P2382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Latifi, as Judge Bonomy explained to you, the Court and -- the Judges and the Defence have read your statement and your transcript in the Milosevic case, so today I would only be going over some limited points with you, to clarify those points. We will not go through your entire testimony again. First thing I'd like to ask you is whether you have done your military service.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then from your village to Pristina -- to Prizren, how far is that?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It's 11 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In what direction, generally, if you are -- if you are in your village of Pirana, what direction is Prizren?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: My village is on the main road Prizren-Gjakova. It's found on the first 11 kilometres, that is, 11 kilometres away from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: North or south?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: North.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You describe in your statement, on the second page, the events that occurred on the 24th of March, 1999, and you say that your village was surrounded by army and Serbian police. I'd like to discuss those units a bit more now in my questions. I'd like, first, to focus on the units you describe as being from the army. What kind of uniforms were the people you describe as being from the army wearing?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The army had a single-colour uniform, what is called SMB, which is olive-grey-green uniform, while the police were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. What were the colour of the police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It was blue and white, mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the vehicles that you saw, some of the vehicles I think you described as being army vehicles, how did they look?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The army vehicles that you mentioned -- in the beginning, the tanks entered; they had tracks. And then there were APCs and Pragas, and they were single-coloured, of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what was the single colour they had?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Olive-green-grey, SMB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were there also vehicles that you think belonged to the police?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The police had some Pinzgauers, a kind of a truck or a van, and also smaller vehicles. There was also a bus, a civilian bus from which they got off. They got off at the entrance of the village, at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you saw them get out of the bus, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes. You could see very clearly from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the colour of the vehicles you just described, that were belonging to the police, what was that?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Blue. Some of them looked darker, darker blue, but there were not many police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the Pinzgauer that you referred to, could you describe how that looked, a little more.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It was blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did it look? You said it was a truck or a van. Did it have any other weapons? What made you identify it as a Pinzgauer?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Well, a Pinzgauer resembles a van. It's closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Had you seen that kind of vehicle before?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where had you seen them?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Because they moved regularly, my house is very close to the main road and those vehicles would go on that main road; not only those but other vehicles as well. There were these blue police vehicles but also other smaller vehicles with the same colour, and they would go regularly on the main road. But they also moved on buses, civilian buses, and civilian cars, civilian trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you specifically say that some of the cars were Pinzgauers, I'm trying find out why you say that. How are you able to identify the cars as being Pinzgauers?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Well, I could tell they were that because of the colour, and the people on them were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You also, in the same paragraph, describe that you saw the houses of your village burn. Where were you when you saw the houses burn?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In the same house I was that morning, in my cousin's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where in the house were you when you could see the houses burn?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The house is in the outskirts of the village, and the Pirane-Reti road is a dirt road, the houses in Pirane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where in the house where you, what room?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I observed from the roof, under the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And from there did you have a view of the village?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Most of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Approximately how many houses do you think you could see burn from that place?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In the beginning there were these kinds of shells. They came from Landovica. The army was stationed there. One of those shells fell 200 metres away from the house where I was; the other one, a little further. While about ten minutes later the first house in the village started to burn. It was close to the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the houses start to burn because of shelling that came from outside the village, or were there people in the village setting the houses alight?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No. It was the police people, because in the beginning the army convoy left the village in the road Pirane-Reti, and then the police were behind them. They went to the mosque -- we went to the mosque and we could see the police burning houses; while the shelling, I would like to say, the minaret of the mosque was damaged that day because of a shell that fell on the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you saw the police actually set light -- set fire to a house, where were you located when you saw that, when you saw the policemen?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In the attic, under the roof in that house; I was for two hours there. So they had not come close to our houses yet, to where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But from where you were located, could you see the policemen?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw. One of the houses that you saw being set alight, could you describe what you actually saw, if you start describing the policemen.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Well, they had some kind of a gun in their hands, and they would shoot that gun and the house then was on fire. And you could see the smoke and the flames. I had never seen such a gun before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And approximately how many houses did you see that happen to?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: During those two hours, about 15 houses. I could see the smoke coming out of them. But when we left the village - because at 8.00, we left the village, as danger was approaching - we went in the direction of Serbica. So half of the village was burned that day, and the next day they started burning it again. One person in Serbica had a pair of binoculars and we could follow what was happening. There was a truck, Zastava, and there were no people there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So did you actually look in the binoculars yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as all the other events are described in your statement, I'm not going to ask you to elaborate more on this, but I have a question that relates both to your statement and something you said in the Milosevic case. Just to make sure that we understand correctly, are you saying that initially, when you had left the town, where you sought refuge, you were protected by the Serb population. Is that a fair way to describe your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: When we went to the village of Serbica, after some sniper shot from a Serb house, Xhafer Elshani was killed and Mehmet Elshani was wounded. They were at the head of the convoy. And then we stayed there in a meadow. Some Serbs from the village, together with some Albanians, told us to get shelter, to go somewhere and not stay outside. So we went inside and the shots stopped immediately. And the villagers said that the Serbs helped -- it was the Serb villagers that said: "We helped for you not to be killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And two last questions. You describe that the chief of the police of Prizren came and said that those who were not originally from Serbica would have to leave the village. Did you, yourself, see the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No, I did not see him personally, but he had given an order to some leaders of the village and they gave us his message. And they came, from house to house, to tell us that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the leaders of the village, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: One of them was Albanian and two were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The last thing I would like to clarify is: You explain in your statement that you -- in a stream behind the house of Mejdi Elshani, in Pirane, in that stream, the police were burying bodies. Did you actually see the bodies being buried?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I saw that they were working on the site, but I also saw that there were three bodies that were thrown down there. But when we went there later, we did not find any bodies, and the ground had been flattened. I remember three bodies in black sacks that were thrown in, plastic black sacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know there were bodies in the sacks?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Well, we could see they were carrying them. It was two people carrying one sack, at both ends. Whether the bodies were Albanian or what they were, I don't know. But several people still remain missing in Pirane, and we went to look for the bodies at that place. We went also to another area animals were buried, but we didn't find any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Latifi. That finishes my questions at this stage for you.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Latifi, what was the date on which you saw this happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, the date was the 27th or the 28th of March, one of these dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the next paragraph of your statement, you say: "On one day I saw two police trucks on the road from Krusha with many bodies inside. I do not know where did they take them." Now, what's the full name of the place that you call Krusha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The full name is Krusha e Madhe, greater Krusha. The trucks came from Krusha e Madhe. They came in the direction of the mosque, and later I heard that they went in the direction of the Drin River. And I think they were burned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how do you know that there were bodies inside the vehicle or the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the back part of the truck, the tarpaulin was a little bit open and there were two legs hanging down. And the truck was so heavily loaded. And you could see that blood was dripping from the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What day was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28th of March, at about 12.00, was the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll follow the indictment, and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk -- oh, sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Latifi, my name is Tomislav Visnjic, appearing for General Dragoljub Ojdanic. I have a few questions for you. You mention in your statement that the situation in the village calmed down somewhere from September 1998 onwards. My first question relates to a period before that. In fact, maybe it's better to ask a general question. Are you aware, Mr. Latifi, that any of your fellow citizens from Pirana was kidnapped in 1998 or 1999 by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I haven't heard of this for this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is the name -- I'll ask you now. Is the name Hazer Tarjani, from Pirana, familiar?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Hazer Tarjani; it's Hazir or Hazer Tarjani. I heard that he disappeared during this period of time. I don't know who kidnapped him, but when he was found, he was buried among -- in the presence of his friends, who honoured him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when he was found?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I think he was found last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that, together with Muret Rrustemi -- sorry, Hida Popaj from Bela Crkva, Bedri Bedrisa from Brestovac village, Besnik Kosnatija from Prizren, and Hasan Morina from Senovac village, he was kidnapped by the KLA, interrogated in Retimlje village and later liquidated by the same organisation. You never heard of that?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No. As I said earlier, I don't know who kidnapped them. And as for Hazir Tarjani, I know he went missing for some time and that he was later found, and that he was buried with honours. The other persons you mentioned, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "he was buried with honours"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was buried with the honours of the co-villagers. There were many family and friends who paid homage. He was not a bad person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So we are still dealing with your statement where you said that from September 1998 the situation in the village improved. I would like to ask you if you are familiar with an incident from November 1998 wherein the KLA attacked a convoy of police vehicles in your village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I please ask that Exhibit 3D139, page 2, be prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of this?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I haven't heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Latifi, from sometime in November, you used to see the Kosovo Verification Mission and its representatives in or around your village. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Their members were always moving around, but I never came across them, I never had any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 3D139, page 2. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the exhibit, I would just like to remind the witness, this is a Kosovo Verification Mission report in which we can read that, on the main route between Prizren and Djakovica, the KLA attacked an MUP patrol with a rocket-launcher which resulted in wounding of the two policemen. At that time you were in your village, weren't you? That was on the 14th of November, 1998. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please see page 2.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I was there on that particular date or not. I have not heard about this specific case that you're mentioning. As for the Verification Mission report, you should ask their members about it because I personally don't have any knowledge of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you leave your village in that period for a few days at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now please see 3D136, page 1.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Whenever we would see forces in movement or, for example, during the Rahovec offensive, we did not stay in our house for a period of ten days. And in my everyday life and work, I could have been in Prizren or elsewhere and that's why I haven't heard of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to remind you, though, that on the 15th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the second half of this exhibit, please, the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of November, the Verification Mission attended this scene, that is the road close to your village, or rather, the road that goes through your village, and they reported on a vehicle of the MUP which had been damaged. They also found bloodstains. Does this jog your memory in any way, Mr. Latifi?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Latifi, are you familiar with an event of the 18th of January, 1999, when the KLA threatened the workers of the Kosovo vino company in the vineyards to the north of your village?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also please have 3D137 put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The wine factory is near the village. Some co-villagers and some of my cousins were employed there. I have not heard that anyone was attacked there; however, on the 24th of March, an Albanian worker was killed there by the forces. I've heard about this incident; I didn't see it myself. He was killed outside the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll try to refresh your memory. On the 18th of January --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down. Paragraph 5. I think this is another document. D137, we had it on the screen a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Latifi, you should be able to remember this document, because after that the Serbs stopped working in the vineyards because the KLA appeared in the vicinity and they were threatened; that's why they stopped working. And the OSCE reported on this in their report of the 18th of January, 1999. You say that quite a number of your -- well, you still claim you don't know of this event?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The factory was still working. It was open until the first -- the last day before the NATO air-strikes began. People were still going to work there, and I think they received their last salary just before the NATO air-strikes began. A neighbour of mine told me that he paid the electricity bill from the money of his last salary, and I'm sure of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The winery was open, but the people dare not go into the vineyards to work. But since you're quite familiar with what took place at the winery, could we please show 3D134, page 8 to the witness. Mr. Latifi, did you know that in February of that same year, the KLA, carrying infantry weapons, entered the perimeter of the Kosovo vino company and at gunpoint they seized official weaponry from the security workers of the company?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be 3D134, paragraph 163.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You don't know about this at all?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I have not heard about it. As for the weapons that you say the security workers had, to my knowledge, I don't think they had weapons. I'm talking about the time earlier. And the later period, it could be so, but that I don't know. I'm just speaking about the times earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You're trying to tell me that, prior to that, the security workers were not issued with any weapons. What do you mean by "previously" or "prior to that"?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I will clarify. The security workers, in the past, did not have weapons. I worked there for three weeks, when you pick the grapes, during that period, and I haven't seen security workers with weapons during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the season in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Before 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get Exhibit 147, page 4, ready; 3D147, that is. I'll repeat. Exhibit 140, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the KLA kidnapped Ymer Xhafiqi, your co-villager? They took him from his house on the 9th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I heard that Ymer Xhafiqi went missing. I do not know who abducted him. He was a security worker at that time; he worked at the police customs office in the MUP. And his body has not been found to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you did hear of some of your co-villagers being abducted.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: That's what the story was that day, but as I said, I don't know who abducted him. And I only know about Ymer Xhafiqi. I don't know of any other persons kidnapped or abducted from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of that the same day or later? Do you remember any such similar event?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: This is a separate incident. I heard two days later that he was abducted. Two days before that I was in Prizren. I was looking after an uncle of mine who was ill. I remember this very well. And when I returned to the village, I heard that Ymer went missing, that he was abducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you are telling me that, for the two days, you were not in the village, on the 9th and 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It was in March; I don't remember the date. But I wasn't in the village during those two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that his wife testified, she confirmed that he had been abducted by the KLA, and that after that his family wasn't favourably looked upon by the other co-villagers for having reported that incident to the police. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please prepare Exhibit D141.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: His wife has a right to report that incident, because I think she was on the spot when that happened. She was in the car with him. But I don't agree with what you said, that they were not favourably looked upon by the other co-villagers. As a family, we always had good relations with this family and with other families in the village. I don't think that the co-villagers looked upon her unfavourably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just two other questions. I can see here that you actually know how he came to be abducted. You say that she was in the same vehicle with him. How come you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: She stated this herself and her son as well. We were in Serbica together at that time. We had good relations between us. This is how we know. When I asked his son, "Who abducted your father," he gave me the same answer, that he didn't know. We were in a cafe, in the village, having a drink together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have Exhibit D141 shown to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3. I have just one more question and then I'm finished concerning this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is another Kosovo Verification Mission report in which one can read that, due to that kidnapping, 60 percent of the women and children left the village. Did you know about that? Did you know that because of that abduction 60 per cent of the women and children of the village left the village and spent at least one night out in the open or outside the village?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No, I never said this. I don't remember myself saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I know you didn't say that, but I'm asking you whether you heard of this, whether you know of the 60 per cent of women and children who left the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Which village do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your village, Pirana.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: This is not true. Not only children and women, but men, women, and children left in the direction of Mamusha and another part in the direction of Serbica. And not only 60 per cent but about 80 per cent of the population left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the 9th and 10th of March. On those two days, did 60 per cent of the population of your village leave the village? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is my last question for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe I've noted it wrongly. Was it the 9th of March, 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1999, Your Honours. All the reports pertain to 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Latifi, we have to stop there for today because another case comes into this court for the afternoon, and we have to resume your evidence tomorrow. For that purpose, you need to be back here to continue giving evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Meanwhile, it's very important that you don't discuss your evidence with anybody, and that means either the evidence you've given already or the evidence you will still have to give, or may give, later tomorrow. You can talk about anything else you wish with whoever you want, but you must not discuss the evidence. Now you'll be shown where to go, and we'll see you again tomorrow morning. Please leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will have it in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
